title: Can Blockchain Decentralise Money, Contracts, and Finance?
text:

The goal of the first blockchain, Bitcoin, was to decentralise money, by registering it on a ledger maintained by independent network nodes and managing its supply by an automatic protocol, without any intervention of intermediaries. Relying on a more sophisticated programming language, Ethereum extended decentralisation to contracts, implemented as programs deployed on blockchain, automatically executed once prespecified conditions were met. This report surveys the technological foundations of blockchain, such as cryptographic tools and blockchain protocols, and discusses under which conditions it is incentive-compatible for nodes to follow the prescribed protocol. The report also discusses the economic importance of the decentralisation of money, contracts, and markets, as well as the problems and challenges faced by blockchain decentralisation. It argues that the adoption of blockchain and the value of cryptocurrencies reflect the economic value of blockchain and of the development on blockchain of an array of financial services, relying on tokens and smart contracts. Decentralisation requires coordination between agents who do not know each other, and creates the risk of coordination failures. A challenge for blockchain is to design protocols that are immune to coordination problems. Another challenge is to connect the ‘cryptosphere’ to the physical world – to enlarge the set of transactions which blockchain technology can facilitate and develop new use cases. Moreover, while blockchain seeks to circumvent opportunistic intermediaries, decentralised finance has led to the rise of a new category of intermediaries. In this context, problems arising in standard markets re-emerge in novel guises: adverse selection costs reappear in the form of ‘impermanent loss’, while front running reappears in the form of ‘sandwich attacks’. These problems are magnified by the fact that some of the new blockchain intermediaries hold a very large share of the market, which can be interpreted as a return to centralisation.
